title: How PilotStack Evaluates Software: Scoring, Sources, and Limitations
description: How PilotStack records software information, calculates ratings, handles uncertain facts, and keeps editorial decisions separate from commercial relationships.
body:
A software review is useful only when readers can understand what a rating means, where factual claims come from, and what has not been independently verified. This article explains the process PilotStack documents for its software coverage and the limits readers should keep in mind. We distinguish recorded information and vendor-published facts from hands-on testing; a published score should not be interpreted as proof that our team independently tested every product in a live environment.

## 1. Define the decision a page should support
We organize coverage around software categories and common buying decisions. The goal is to help readers compare relevant criteria, understand trade-offs, and identify what they should verify for their own team. A shortlist is a starting point, not a universal recommendation: requirements, budget, region, security obligations, and existing systems can change which product is a good fit.

## 2. Record facts with clear limits
Our pages draw on the structured information held in the PilotStack dataset, vendor documentation, and published pricing pages. Product facts can change, and the presence of a value in a record does not by itself mean it was independently confirmed recently. Where a fact lacks a source or confidence is insufficient, the page should omit it or identify it as unverified rather than present it as certain. Readers should confirm current prices, plan limits, feature availability, and contractual terms with the vendor before making a purchase.

## 3. Calculate ratings consistently
The published methodology uses nine recorded category scores on a 1-to-5 scale. The overall rating is the arithmetic mean of those nine scores, rounded to one decimal place. This makes the calculation reproducible from the displayed inputs, but it does not remove the limitations of the underlying evidence or mean every buyer should weight the criteria equally. Teams should prioritize the categories that matter most to their workflows and risk tolerance.

## 4. Keep information consistent across pages
PilotStack reuses recorded product fields in multiple parts of the site so the same value is not intentionally changed from one page to another. A consistent record reduces contradictions, but it is not a guarantee that the original source is current or complete. Dates shown on a page indicate the recorded content update; they should not be read as a promise that every product claim was rechecked on that date.

## 5. Separate editorial decisions from commercial relationships
Commercial arrangements must not determine editorial scores, rankings, or inclusion criteria. Where referral links or other commercial relationships apply, they should be disclosed. Paid promotion, if used, must be distinguishable from editorial content and must not be described as an independent recommendation. The published methodology and disclosure pages explain these principles in more detail.

## Corrections and limitations
Software features, pricing, security terms, and product limits can change. Readers should report suspected errors through the site's contact page with the affected URL and supporting details. When a correction is warranted, the record and its displayed update information should be revised. We do not claim that every product is tested hands-on, that vendors approve our opinions, or that every data point has been independently verified. The useful question is not simply whether a page has a score, but whether its evidence and limitations are clear enough for readers to make their own informed decision.

For the current scoring rules and sourcing policy, read the main methodology page. If you spot a factual error or a missing qualification, please contact us so it can be reviewed.
